Senses.Explanation: This label identifies the verse attached to a lineage handoff. Biographies place it after an entrustment to Ananda or Upagupta, while Jie’an asks why lamp records stop printing such verses below Mazu. Upagupta’s biography says he is ordained, receives the teaching-eye, and is then given the transmission verse before the preceding patriarch withdraws. The record of Mahakasyapa likewise introduces a four-line verse immediately after his charge that Ananda guard the teaching entrusted to him. Jie’an Jin turns the documentary pattern into a public challenge: if the buddhas and patriarchs all have transmission verses printed in lamp records, why are none printed below Mazu—were they absent or withheld? Shiyu Mingfang writes a transmission verse during an explicit succession scene. The label therefore names an institutional verse-object, not every verse about transmission.

Senses.Explanation: At year’s coldest end, a mountain burns: Xianglin Chengyuan’s answer to “what is the matter beneath the patch robe?” (如何是衲衣下事). Xuedou Chongxian’s later verse keeps the collision visible—cold cranes in the pines and people walking through snow beside the burning mountain—and calls it difficult. Gulin Qingmao and Yuanwu Keqin raise the same answer and those winter lines; Lizhong Cheng later writes of the mountain fire glowing red while an icy place becomes warm. These comments establish the cold/fire conjunction and the inherited case, but do not assign the line a hidden paraphrase.

Senses.Explanation: The high stride on Vairocana’s crown marks speech that refuses deference to named buddhas: an unnamed monastic questioner, Yuanwu Keqin, and Huoqiu Guicai each place the phrase in that setting. An unnamed monastic questioner joins the phrase to cutting off the throat of the Buddha before all buddhas, treating Shakyamuni as a maid and Maitreya as a servant; Feiyin answers, “half a nostril.” Yuanwu Keqin says that even someone who strides on Vairocana’s crown and does not submit to Shakyamuni must become speechless before the matter he presents. Huoqiu Guicai says that awakening at his stated point lets one sit atop transformation buddhas and stride on Vairocana’s crown.

Senses.Explanation: It is overwhelmingly paired with "walk on the floor of the deepest sea" (深深海底行). In a recorded biography, Zhaojue asks a student, "stand atop the highest peak; walk on the floor of the deepest sea—how do you understand it?" The student awakens at the words and says, "my heels are nailed fast" (釘殺脚跟也); Zhaojue then raises the whisk and asks another question. The paired line also serves as a direct answer in public interview and as an instruction to an assembly: "at this point it is just right to stand atop the highest peak and walk on the floor of the deepest sea" (到恁麼地，正好高高峰頂立，深深海底行). Another address distributes the pair across dates: before the twenty-fifth, the ocean-floor line; after it, the summit line; on the twenty-fifth, all ten directions cut off. Zen turns impossible vertical extremes into a fixed paired demand, question, answer, and biographical exchange; the corpus does not require this entry to decode the image further.

Senses.Explanation: Silent for a long while records a sustained pause that can itself become the action questioned, demanded, imitated, or rejected in a public exchange. A recorded master asks a questioner how he understands prolonged silence; the questioner answers that he takes it simply as prolonged silence and is rejected. A later questioner remains silent after a question and receives the verdict that dead water holds no dragon. Biographies and formal instruction also quote teachers demanding that someone manifest what is at issue without sound or form through such a pause. The phrase therefore marks observable timing, not blank missing text.

Senses.Explanation: Silent illumination is a disputed label in the Zen records. Hongzhi Zhengjue joins silence and illumination affirmatively, saying that ‘one of silent illumination is numinous’ and that the autumn sky clears at the place of silent illumination. Dahui Zonggao uses the compound critically for people he opposes and says that, although he does not permit it, everyone must face the wall. Hanyue Fazang defines it critically as taking a bright, numinous object found while sitting to be oneself. Shanhui Huan places it beside withered Zen as something difficult to cure.
